newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tokyo stocks likely to slide, HK to hit new highs.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks likely to slide, HK to hit new highs.

text.p: Tokyo stocks are likely to slide in the coming week after the Nikkei's fall below the key 20,500 level, while Hong Kong shares are expected to reach new highs after the Hang Seng hit a record close, analysts said.

But the rest of Asia's bourses are looking at a lacklustre week, highlighted by the U.S. presidential and congressional elections on Tuesday, as they await something to move the markets, the experts say.
The Bangkok, Colombo, Kuala Lumpur, Taipei and Dhaka markets could edge up, the analysts said, while the Singapore bourse may drift down. Other exchanges are looking at mixed trading.
TOKYO - Stocks are likely to keep hunting for a floor with the benchmark Nikkei 225 moving between 20,000 and 21,000 and carrying the risk of momentary dips below.
"Despite the Nikkei's fall below the 20,500 level this (past) week, there doesn't seem to be a feeling that the market has hit the bottom," Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities said.
"Foreign investor selling, which had been forcing domestic investors onto the sidelines lately, is abating but they are not quite ready to buy yet," he said.
Brokers said the formation of a new Japanese government in the week ahead and the U.S. elections are likely to keep investors on the sidelines.
On Friday, the Nikkei 225 ended up 166.20 points, or 0.81 percent, at 20,633,06, unable to recoup the loss of more than 870 points the previous week. It closed at 20,739.97 on Friday.

HONG KONG - Stocks are poised to reach new record levels following Friday's record close on the Hang Seng index and encouraging U.S. economic data that pushed the long bond yield lower, analysts said.

"We are hoping that the Hang Seng index will move above the previous intra-day high and stay above that at the closing," said Alex Tang, head of research at Yamaichi International. The intra-day record high was on October 16 at 12,602.34 points.
The Hang Seng rose 51.71 points to a record 12,529.27 on Friday. It gained 140.89 points, or 1.14 percent, for the week.
BANGKOK - Stocks are expected to fall on uncertainty ahead of Thailand's November 17 general election, a perceived increase in market risk and a lack of fresh positive news, analysts said.
"I would have thought trade will be very light, there won't be a lot of company results and a lot of people are sitting back waiting," said Richard Henderson, of Krungthai Thanakit Plc.
The SET Index closed at 912.52 points Friday, down 25.78 ponts over the week on sluggish trade worth 13.16 billion baht.
COLOMBO - Sri Lanka stocks are seen edging up due to a lack of sellers who are waiting for higher prices, brokers said.
The All Share index closed on Friday at 610.98, compared to 608.04 points two weeks ago.
"The All Share should rise because buyers have no option but to move up," said broker Shanil Perara of Lanka Securities.
JAKARTA - Jakarta share prices are seen mixed in relatively slow trading as the market remains focused on the Bank Negara Indonesia initial public offering, brokers said.
"The IPO of BNI has captured the market's attention for the last week and it might continue in the coming week," one said.
On Friday, the Jakarta Composite Index closed at 570.66 points against last week's close of 571.34 points.
KUALA LUMPUR - Analysts and dealers expect the current uptrend to continue.

"In the medium term I expect to see the market still trending upwards. We are not expecting any major economic data this week," said Lim Soo Chong of HLG Securities, implying that the fundamentals for the market should not change significantly.
The Composite Index of 100 leading stocks ended on Friday at 1,172.48, down 0.47 points for the week. The Second Board index of smaller issues closed at 634.51, up 3.15 week-on-week.
MANILA - Manila stocks are seen consolidating after a three-day technical rebound, analysts said.
The main index fell 110.44 points last Monday to a seven-month low of 2,852.16 before the recovery set in.
"It's a dead cat bounce. There is an initial spurt in the market but trading is happening in a negative environment," said Felix Barrientos, a trader at ING Barings Securities.
The index closed on Thursday at 2,964, up 1.4 points week-on-week. The market was closed on Friday for a holiday.
SINGAPORE - Brokers said key stocks such as SIA, Fraser & Neave, and Singapore Press Holdings would show the way.
Most doubted the market would rally given the lack of buying incentives amid the absence of fresh news, and said investors would watch the U.S. elections for any impact on Wall Street.
The Straits Times Industrials Index ended down 15.06 points at 2,068.17 on Friday against 2,077.20 a week earlier.
SEOUL - Seoul shares are expected to be mixed as bargain hunting struggles with margin loan pressures, brokers said.
"I expect the technical rebound to continue, but it will be limited by selling to pay back loans for margin trading," Lee Ha-yong of Hyundai Securities said.
Margin loans are at about three trillion won, while customer deposits at brokerage houses lag behind at 2.7 trillion.
On Friday, the composite index closed at 767.87, down 25.91 points (3.26 percent) from the previous week's close of 793.78.
SYDNEY - Australian shares are seen starting cautiously, likely dominated by continued speculation about a local rate cut after the Reserve Bank of Australia meeting on Tuesday.

"The outlook is mostly positive, especially if base metal prices continue to firm. The risk lies with any major weakness on Wall Street or if the Reserve Bank doesn't move on rates," a dealer at a Sydney-based brokerage said.
The All Ordinaries index closed down 10.8 points at 2,339.4 on Friday after gaining just 5.3 points over the week.

TAIPEI - Share prices are expected to rise following the government announcement on Friday that it would let Taiwan's T$188 billion state labour insurance fund invest up to 30 percent of its holdings in the island's stock market.
"The decision will convince many investors that the government still supports the stock market," said Oliver Fang, an analyst of National Securities.
But brokers said the lack of leading market sectors would prevent sharp rises. Blue chip electronics that rose on profits in the first three quarters were expected face consolidation.
The index ended at 6,455.11 on Friday compared with 6,458.91 a week earlier. It is expected to move in the 6,400-6,500 range.
BOMBAY - Indian shares are seen in a tight range with political factors overwhelming good company results.
"There's talk of a possible snap poll next year," said one trader. "It's unsettling buyers."
The Bombay Stock Exchange top-30 share index fell 102.09 points, or 3.14 percent, to 3,148.57.
DHAKA - Stocks gained heavily in the past week, spurred by good corporate news. Prices soared every session after Apex Foods announced a bonus and Amam Sea Food offered rights shares.
"Expectations are flying high after the offers were made. The bullish trend is likely to continue until late November when annual meetings of many companies are scheduled," a broker said.
Dhaka stocks rose a record 792.49 points for the week to close at 2,986.29 on Thursday.
